group.passage: For thousands of years, people who have lost an arm or a leg have searched for ways to carry on with daily life. The seven entries below, taken from a museum timeline, show how artificial limbs have changed, from carved wood to hands that respond to the body.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: About 3,000 years ago: Egypt
passage_parts.text: An artificial big toe made of wood and leather was found still attached to the foot of a woman buried near Luxor. Its three pieces were joined so that it could bend, and clear signs of wear suggest that she really walked on it instead of wearing it only for show.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Around 300 BC: Italy
passage_parts.text: A Roman leg made of bronze and wood was discovered in a grave at Capua, in southern Italy. The original was later destroyed in a bombing raid during the Second World War, so today only a copy remains.

passage_parts.label: C
passage_parts.title: The 1500s: Europe
passage_parts.text: Craftsmen who normally made locks, clocks and guns began producing hands of iron, brass and wood. The fingers could not move on their own: the wearer used the other hand to push them into position and pressed a button to release them.

passage_parts.label: D
passage_parts.title: The 1500s: France
passage_parts.text: Ambroise Paré, a French army surgeon, designed a mechanical hand that used springs and catches; one was worn into battle by an army captain. He also created a leg with a knee that could be locked for standing and bent when the wearer wished.

passage_parts.label: E
passage_parts.title: 1861: United States
passage_parts.text: Early in the American Civil War, a cannonball shattered the leg of a young soldier named James Hanger. Frustrated with the simple wooden peg he was given, he shut himself in his room for months and carved a new leg from barrel staves, with a knee that could bend. He later took out a patent and founded a company that still exists.

passage_parts.label: F
passage_parts.title: The 1980s: United States
passage_parts.text: Van Phillips, who had lost part of a leg in a waterskiing accident, studied how the back leg of a cheetah stores energy as the animal lands. His carbon foot bends like a spring under the wearer’s weight and then pushes back, and versions of it are now used by athletes around the world.

passage_parts.label: G
passage_parts.title: Today
passage_parts.text: Inside some of today’s artificial limbs are small motors that get their power from a battery. Sensors pick up tiny electrical signals from the muscles left in the arm, so the wearer can open and close the fingers by tightening those muscles. Such hands are a far cry from the iron hands of the 1500s, and cheap 3D printers now let people make simple ones at home.

questions.stem:
Which of the following can be inferred from the timeline? From (A) to (H) below, choose the ONES that are true.
請選出正確的選項，並劃記在答題卷作答區內。（多選題，4分）

options.A: Some early artificial limbs were made for real use, not just looks.
options.B: The oldest limb in the timeline was made entirely of metal.
options.C: The first mechanical hands could move their fingers by themselves.
options.D: Not every advance came from a doctor or a scientist.
options.E: The Roman leg survives today in its original form.
options.F: Carbon blades give disabled runners an unfair advantage.

translation_zh.text:
幾千年來，失去手臂或腿的人一直在尋找繼續過日常生活的方法。下面七則條目取自一份博物館的時間軸，說明義肢如何改變：從雕刻的木頭，一路到能回應身體的手。

A 約三千年前：埃及
人們發現一根以木頭和皮革製成的義肢大腳趾，仍然連在一位葬在路克索附近的女性腳上。它的三個部分接合在一起，可以彎曲，而明顯的磨損痕跡顯示，她真的用它走路，而不只是戴著好看。

B 約西元前 300 年：義大利
在義大利南部卡普阿的一座墳墓裡，發現了一條以青銅和木頭製成的羅馬義腿。原件後來在第二次世界大戰的一次空襲中被毀，所以如今只剩一件複製品。

C 1500 年代：歐洲
平常製作鎖、時鐘和槍的工匠，開始用鐵、黃銅和木頭製作義手。這些手指無法自己活動：配戴者要用另一隻手把它們推到定位，再按下按鈕把它們放開。

D 1500 年代：法國
法國軍醫安布魯瓦茲‧帕雷設計了一種使用彈簧和卡榫的機械手，曾有一位陸軍上尉戴著它上戰場。他也設計了一種義腿，膝蓋在站立時可以鎖住，配戴者想彎的時候也能彎曲。

E 1861 年：美國
美國南北戰爭初期，一顆砲彈打碎了年輕士兵詹姆斯‧漢格的腿。他對分到的簡單木樁腿感到挫折，於是把自己關在房間裡好幾個月，用木桶板刻出一條新腿，膝蓋還能彎曲。他後來取得專利，並創立了一家至今仍在營運的公司。

F 1980 年代：美國
范‧菲利浦斯在一次滑水意外中失去了部分的腿，他研究獵豹的後腿在落地時如何儲存能量。他的碳纖維義足在配戴者的體重下會像彈簧一樣彎曲，然後再彈回去；如今世界各地的運動員都在使用它的各種版本。

G 今日
現今有些義肢裡裝著小馬達，從電池取得動力。感測器接收殘肢肌肉發出的微弱電訊號，配戴者只要收緊那些肌肉，就能讓手指張開、合起。這樣的手和 1500 年代的鐵手相比已經天差地遠，而便宜的 3D 印表機現在也讓人們能在家裡做出簡單的義手。

A Roman leg of bronze and wood from about 300 BC found in a grave at Capua, southern Italy; the original was destroyed in a WWII bombing raid and only a copy remains.
In the 1500s, locksmiths, clockmakers and gunsmiths made hands of iron, brass and wood; the wearer pushed the fingers into position with the other hand and pressed a button to release them.
Ambroise Paré, a French army surgeon, designed a mechanical hand with springs and catches worn into battle by an army captain, and a leg with a lockable knee.

In 1861 a cannonball shattered James Hanger’s leg; frustrated with his peg leg, he spent months in his room carving a leg with a bending knee from barrel staves; he later patented it and founded a company that still exists.
